OVERVIEW

[1] This decision is about XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), who is a citizen of Kenya. She claims that she faces persecution by criminal gangs who were involved in human trafficking of XXXX. She claims that she was targeted by them when she refused to alter records after witnessing the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX while working as a XXXX at a XXXX, and because she attended a community meeting and spoke about female genital mutilation (FGM) and women's rights as well as the incident when the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which found that she had not credibly established her allegations because of omissions, inconsistencies, evolving evidence and lack of corroboration; delay in claiming and abandonment of her claim made in the United States (US); because she did not rebut the presumption of state protection; and because she has two viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Nairobi and Mombasa. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its findings, arguing that her ability to testify was negatively impacted by the recent death of her employer; that the RPD rushed her lawyer in his closing submissions; that it failed to consider the objective country condition evidence and her explanations regarding her corroborative evidence; because in its findings regarding state protection, it failed to consider her good reasons to fear reporting the crimes to the police; and that it erred in finding that she has a viable IFA in Kenya. Based on my review of the evidence and arguments, I find that the RPD did not err, and uphold its credibility findings, as I agree that the Appellant's evidence was vague, evolving, inconsistent and lacking expected corroboration, and find that this is not explained by her psychological state. I also agree that her abandonment of her US asylum claim further diminishes the credibility of her subjective fear. I find that the issue of credibility is determinative in the Appellant's claim and have no need to address the RPD's findings and the Appellant's arguments regarding state protection and IFA in Kenya. I find that she has not established that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
DECISION

[2] I dismiss the appeal and uphold the RPD's decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

[7] The Appellant submits a consultation note dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 and a progress note dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 by Dr. XXXX XXXX, psychiatrist, as new evidence in support of her appeal. She also submits a letter from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, which states that she works as a caregiver for the Appellant's former client's husband, and that she is familiar with the Appellant's close relationship with the family. The Appellant argues that the new evidence should be admitted as follows:
We would like to address the Member's Preliminary Issue concerning the appellant's late request to reconvene the hearing because of the trauma she faced on the day of the hearing, arising from the death of her employer, Mrs. XXXX, for whom she was the live-in caregiver. We agree that the Member was justified in denying the application because (i) the appellant did not provide any psychological or medical reports about her mental health status before, during, or after the hearing, and (ii) neither the appellant nor her counsel indicate that she had any issues about testifying before the panel owing to the death of her employer in Canada XXXX days before the hearing. However, these reports have since been obtained and are attached...for the RAD to appreciate the appellant's state of mind during the hearing. As well, there is a letter...from the appellant's relief caregiver that informs the IRB about the close relationship the appellant had with the deceased patient and the appellant's troubled state of mind at that time. For these reasons, we request that the RAD should hold a hearing under section 110(6) of the IRPA.3

[8] The Appellant's previous representative stated in her letter requesting that the hearing be re-convened that the Appellant did not previously disclose the death of her employer or her mental state until after her hearing because she "is from a culture where she does not openly express her emotions, and it did not occur to her to divulge this death at her refugee hearing...."4

[9] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)5 provides that appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims, that was not reasonably available, or that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented at the time of the rejection of the claims. If the new evidence meets one of the criteria set out in subsection 110(4), then the RAD may assess its admissibility further based on its credibility, relevance and newness.6

[10] I accept that the consultation report and letter from the relief caregiver meet the criteria for new evidence, as the death of the Appellant's employer took place just before the hearing, and I accept that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented this evidence at the time of the rejection of her claim. It is also new evidence and relevant to her claim.

[11] The Appellant also provides an excerpt from an article, Rita Shackel's (and Lucy Fiske's) "Kenya Country Report: Making Justice Work for Women" dated August 2016.7 She makes no argument regarding why this article meets the criteria for acceptance as new evidence but submits that it discusses how Kenyan women participants in the research project highlighted police corruption and ineffectiveness as a key barrier to women accessing justice there. I find that the Appellant has not established that the excerpt from the article meets the criteria for acceptance as new evidence, as it dates back to 2016, and there is no explanation why she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented this evidence at the time of the rejection of her claim.

As I will explain further below, I find that the new evidence does not establish that the credibility issues in her claim were explained by her mental health, and further find that many of the credibility issues identified by the RPD, such as the lack of expected corroboration, are unrelated to her oral testimony.

The panel also granted the representative 10 minutes to gather his thoughts before he made his closing submissions, and a further opportunity at the end of the hearing on the request of the Appellant's legal representative to make a final point.17 Further, the closing submissions provided were extensive, and covered all of the issues in the appeal, including Convention grounds, the Appellant's cultural background and ear injury, caselaw on credibility, specific issues in the evidence regarding omissions and state protection, subjective fear and the Appellant's US refugee claim and delay in claiming, the alleged agents of persecution, objective country condition evidence and citations from the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Kenya, s.97 and generalized risk, state protection and IFA. Finally, the Appellant does not specify what issues were missed or what would have been presented had her representative not been rushed as alleged. I find that the RPD did not rush the Appellant's legal representative's closing submissions as argued by the Appellant.

[21] The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred in paying inadequate attention to the oral submissions made by her counsel, including Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) directives, Federal Court decisions and evidence of forward-looking risk from the NDP. I find, however, that she does not specify what has been ignored, and based on my review, I do not see that the RPD erred in this fashion as argued.
The RPD did not err in its credibility findings

[22] The RPD made a number of findings regarding the credibility of the Appellant's evidence, including that her testimony was vague and evolving; that there were significant inconsistencies and omissions in her evidence; and that she did not provide expected corroboration of her allegations; for example, of the claimed XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, such as media reports, police reports or a support letter from her husband or the mother who was the alleged victim of the crime, whom she claims she had been in touch with while in the US.

[23] With respect to her claim that she spoke out regarding women's health issues and the XXXX XXXX incident, the RPD found that the Appellant was evolving and unclear in her evidence about these allegations and inconsistent in the number of meetings that she spoke at. It found that she initially testified that she spoke only at a Chief's meeting in 2015, but then her evidence evolved to being a speaker six or seven times and then four times.

[24] The Appellant does not specifically challenge this finding, except regarding the issue of the impact of her mental health on her ability to testify, which I have addressed above. I agree with the RPD's inconsistency finding as outlined above, and that the Appellant's vague, evolving and inconsistent evidence regarding her role as a spokesperson on women's health issues, despite the efforts of the panel to prompt her and ask follow-up questions about this allegation, is damaging to the credibility of her allegations.

[25] Regarding her claims about the Chinkororo gang, the alleged agents of persecution, the RPD found that she omitted an allegation that members of the gang confronted her at the community meeting in 2015. It found that she was inconsistent regarding when the alleged threats began, testifying that they started before the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, at the local meeting where she spoke, but in her narrative stated that she came to their attention later after the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident. Further, it found that she did not provide corroborating evidence regarding the existence of the Chinkororo gang.

[26] The Appellant does not specifically challenge these findings except for her general argument that problems in her testimony were caused by her troubled state of mind because of the trauma of her employer's recent death, which I have found has not been established. Based on my review, I agree with the RPD's finding that her evidence about when the alleged threats began was inconsistent, and that there was a lack of corroboration about the Chinkororo gang, and that these factors reduce the credibility of her allegations.

[27] The RPD found that a hand-written letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2018 from an assistant chief's office about unknown people who allegedly attacked her home and "roughing up" her family to be unreliable, as she could not explain why her husband would report this alleged attack to the assistant chief instead of the police; her evidence was inconsistent, as she testified that the men just asked for her, but the letter states that the family was "roughed up;" and it was unclear who "the family" at the home was, as her adult children did not live there.

[28] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in this finding, as she claims that her sons were at the home following the funeral of her colleague, and because of cultural differences and beliefs about police corruption, it was reasonable to report the attack to the chief, who plays a role in maintaining order in the community. Even if this is the case, I agree with RPD's finding that her testimony was inconsistent with the description of the attack in the letter, as she testified that they were not assaulted as follows:

MEMBER: How was your husband harassed? What do you mean by that?
CLAIMANT: How can I put it now? They told him --- they demanded to know where I am. They told him to open the house and then they entered and looked for me. When they didn't find me, they asked him, where is your wife who is the one we want. He told them ---

CLAIMANT: No.

I agree with the RPD and find that this significant inconsistency between the letter and the Appellant's testimony reduces the credibility of this letter.
Delay

[29] The RPD also found that the Appellant's abandonment of her asylum claim in the US after living there for one and a half years also diminished the credibility of her subjective fear. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in this finding, as she did not feel safe or feel she would receive fair treatment there, but I disagree with this argument, and agree with the RPD that the fact that she left the US in the middle of her asylum claim to diminish her credibility. As noted by the Appellant, she had a nursing job there and had a roof over her head, and I find that her claim was ongoing, and she had no immediate fear of deportation or loss of status.
Lack of corroboration

[30] The RPD found that other expected corroboration was lacking, and that other corroborating evidence was unreliable. It found that there was a lack of corroboration of the alleged XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, and that this diminished the credibility of this claim. The Appellant testified that the incident was reported in the media, but provided no corroboration of this incident, and only submitted an article about a similar incident in 2016. In response to this concern, the Appellant testified that she had lost her phone and was unable to contact anyone to obtain corroborating evidence about this incident. She had also testified that she had spoken with the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX while she was in the US in 2018, however, her contact with the mother and her update on the police investigation was omitted from her narrative. Further, although allegedly in contact with her, she did not obtain any corroboration such as a letter or affidavit from her, even though the mother allegedly informed her that the investigation was ongoing, and that one person had been arrested. The RPD did not accept her explanation that she did not know that she should do that because of what she was undergoing.19 I agree with the RPD that the Appellant was inconsistent in her explanation for her lack of corroboration, as she said she could not contact anyone because she had lost her phone, but this was inconsistent with her evidence that she had been in touch with the mother of the XXXX XXXX. I agree that she did not adequately explain why she did not request corroboration of the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, which was central to her claim.

[31] The Appellant argues that the RPD was illogical in noting that the news article provided was "eerily similar" to her own allegations, but even if that was the case, it does not change the fact that she provided no corroboration of this incident, which I find would have been expected.

[32] The RPD made a negative inference from the fact that the Appellant did not provide corroboration from her husband, who was allegedly attacked by unknown people and tried to get corroborating evidence. I agree with this negative inference.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] This decision is about XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), who is a citizen of Kenya. She claims that she faces persecution by criminal gangs who were involved in human trafficking of XXXX. She claims that she was targeted by them when she refused to alter records after witnessing the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX while working as a XXXX at a XXXX, and because she attended a community meeting and spoke about female genital mutilation (FGM) and women's rights as well as the incident when the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which found that she had not credibly established her allegations because of omissions, inconsistencies, evolving evidence and lack of corroboration; delay in claiming and abandonment of her claim made in the United States (US); because she did not rebut the presumption of state protection; and because she has two viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Nairobi and Mombasa. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its findings, arguing that her ability to testify was negatively impacted by the recent death of her employer; that the RPD rushed her lawyer in his closing submissions; that it failed to consider the objective country condition evidence and her explanations regarding her corroborative evidence; because in its findings regarding state protection, it failed to consider her good reasons to fear reporting the crimes to the police; and that it erred in finding that she has a viable IFA in Kenya. Based on my review of the evidence and arguments, I find that the RPD did not err, and uphold its credibility findings, as I agree that the Appellant's evidence was vague, evolving, inconsistent and lacking expected corroboration, and find that this is not explained by her psychological state. I also agree that her abandonment of her US asylum claim further diminishes the credibility of her subjective fear. I find that the issue of credibility is determinative in the Appellant's claim and have no need to address the RPD's findings and the Appellant's arguments regarding state protection and IFA in Kenya. I find that she has not established that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
DECISION
[2] I dismiss the appeal and uphold the RPD's decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
BACKGROUND

[3] The Appellant claims that she is at risk because of threats by criminals involved in human trafficking in XXXX. She claims that in XXXX 2016, she witnessed an incident at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and that she refused her supervisor's demand that she XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to help cover up the crime. She also claims that she spoke at public meetings regarding issues such as FGM, women's health and the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, and that this also led to her fear of persecution. She alleges that on XXXX XXXX, 2016, she was struck from behind, and believes that this was an attempt to silence her about the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident. On XXXX XXXX, 2016, she was called to a meeting held by a local chief, and she spoke out against FGM and the incident with the XXXX. In XXXX 2017, she alleges that she was told by hospital management to report to the police station regarding corruption allegations, but while there she claims that she was sexually assaulted and threatened in response to her public speeches about FGM and the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident. She claims that as a result, in XXXX 2017 she fled to her aunt's home and then to Nairobi. She learned that after she left her aunt's home, people went there to look for her. She fled to the US in XXXX 2017, claimed asylum there, and obtained authorization to work and study. Fearing the political climate and possible deportation, however, she crossed irregularly into Canada in XXXX 2018, and made a new refugee claim here.

[4] Her claim was heard by the RPD on January 10, 2020. On January 28, 2020, the Appellant requested that her hearing be reconvened, as she had now disclosed that her ability to testify at the hearing may have been impacted by her grief and trauma from the death of her employer, for whom the Appellant was a caregiver, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 just before her hearing. In its reasons dated February 11, 2020 the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim. It denied her request to reconvene the hearing, as no medical or psychological evidence was provided in support of her claim that she was traumatized and that this impacted her ability to testify. Further, this issue was not raised during her hearing, nor was there any request to provide post-hearing evidence. The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence lacked credibility because it was evolving and there were omissions and inconsistencies in her evidence, as well as a lack of expected corroboration of her allegations. Further, she had delayed making a refugee claim; did not rebut the presumption of state protection; and had a viable IFA in Kenya.

[5] The Appellant has appealed this decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). She provides new evidence regarding her psychological state after the death of her employer and in support of her claimed close relationship with her and requests an oral hearing. She argues that the RPD erred in its findings as outlined above, arguing that her ability to testify was impacted by the recent death of her employer; that the RPD rushed her lawyer in his closing submissions; that it failed to consider the objective country condition evidence and her explanations regarding her corroborative evidence; that she did not fail to rebut the presumption of state protection, as she had good reason to fear reporting the crimes to the police; and that she does not have a viable IFA in Kenya.
ANALYSIS

[6] As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica,1 the RAD must review RPD decisions on a correctness standard with respect to questions of law and findings of fact (and mixed fact and law). Deference may be required only when the RPD has a meaningful advantage with respect to the assessment of oral evidence.2 In this case, my findings are based on a correctness standard. I find that the RPD was not in an advantageous position regarding the assessment of the Appellant's oral evidence, as I was able to review and clearly understand the record of the hearing.
NEW EVIDENCE

[7] The Appellant submits a consultation note dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 and a progress note dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 by Dr. XXXX XXXX, psychiatrist, as new evidence in support of her appeal. She also submits a letter from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, which states that she works as a caregiver for the Appellant's former client's husband, and that she is familiar with the Appellant's close relationship with the family. The Appellant argues that the new evidence should be admitted as follows:
We would like to address the Member's Preliminary Issue concerning the appellant's late request to reconvene the hearing because of the trauma she faced on the day of the hearing, arising from the death of her employer, Mrs. XXXX, for whom she was the live-in caregiver. We agree that the Member was justified in denying the application because (i) the appellant did not provide any psychological or medical reports about her mental health status before, during, or after the hearing, and (ii) neither the appellant nor her counsel indicate that she had any issues about testifying before the panel owing to the death of her employer in Canada XXXX days before the hearing. However, these reports have since been obtained and are attached...for the RAD to appreciate the appellant's state of mind during the hearing. As well, there is a letter...from the appellant's relief caregiver that informs the IRB about the close relationship the appellant had with the deceased patient and the appellant's troubled state of mind at that time. For these reasons, we request that the RAD should hold a hearing under section 110(6) of the IRPA.3

[8] The Appellant's previous representative stated in her letter requesting that the hearing be re-convened that the Appellant did not previously disclose the death of her employer or her mental state until after her hearing because she "is from a culture where she does not openly express her emotions, and it did not occur to her to divulge this death at her refugee hearing...."4

[9] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)5 provides that appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims, that was not reasonably available, or that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented at the time of the rejection of the claims. If the new evidence meets one of the criteria set out in subsection 110(4), then the RAD may assess its admissibility further based on its credibility, relevance and newness.6

[10] I accept that the consultation report and letter from the relief caregiver meet the criteria for new evidence, as the death of the Appellant's employer took place just before the hearing, and I accept that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented this evidence at the time of the rejection of her claim. It is also new evidence and relevant to her claim.

[11] The Appellant also provides an excerpt from an article, Rita Shackel's (and Lucy Fiske's) "Kenya Country Report: Making Justice Work for Women" dated August 2016.7 She makes no argument regarding why this article meets the criteria for acceptance as new evidence but submits that it discusses how Kenyan women participants in the research project highlighted police corruption and ineffectiveness as a key barrier to women accessing justice there. I find that the Appellant has not established that the excerpt from the article meets the criteria for acceptance as new evidence, as it dates back to 2016, and there is no explanation why she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented this evidence at the time of the rejection of her claim.
ORAL HEARING

[12] The Appellant has requested an oral hearing. Subsection 110(6) of the IRPA provides that the RAD may hold an oral hearing if there is documentary evidence that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this case, I find that her new evidence, while accepted, is not sufficient to justify allowing her appeal, as it does not overcome the credibility concerns in her evidence. As I will explain further below, I find that the new evidence does not establish that the credibility issues in her claim were explained by her mental health, and further find that many of the credibility issues identified by the RPD, such as the lack of expected corroboration, are unrelated to her oral testimony.
The RPD did not err in refusing to re-convene the hearing, and the Appellant has not established that the credibility issues were explained by her mental health

[13] As discussed above, the RPD refused the Appellant's request to re-convene her hearing on the basis of the late disclosure of her employer's recent death and claim that she was traumatized and that this affected her ability to testify at the hearing. The Appellant concedes that the RPD did not err in refusing this request, as this issue was not raised at her hearing, and no psychological or medical evidence was provided at the date of the request. She argues, however, that now that such evidence has been provided, the RAD should consider her mental state and close relationship with her employer and hold a hearing.

[14] Based on my review of this new evidence, I find that the Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that her mental state was responsible for the credibility issues identified by the RPD. I give the opinions provided in the consultation note and progress report limited weight, as it was based on only two telephone interviews, and no treatment or meaningful follow-up was provided by the psychiatrist, indicating that any mental health concerns were not significant. The reports also list a number of contributing factors to any mental health concerns, including incidents dating before and after the Appellant's hearing, indicating that any mental health impacts were not precipitated mainly by the death of the Appellant's employer just before her RPD hearing. In summary, I find the Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that her mental health explains the credibility issues found by the RPD, and that this is not determinative of her appeal. Further, although some of the credibility findings related to the Appellant's testimony, including findings of evolving and unclear testimony, other findings such as omissions and a lack of expected corroboration are unrelated to her testimony and not explained by her mental health condition.

[15] I give the consultation and progress notes only limited weight. They provide a diagnosis/assessment of XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, but I note that they are based only on two telephone interviews, which the psychiatrist concedes limited her ability to carry out a mental status examination,8 and no objective testing was carried out. The psychiatrist is not the Appellant's treating physician and thus had only a limited ability to assess her mental health; she was contacted for the purpose of gathering evidence for the appeal rather than for treatment. No ongoing treatment was provided, which I further find suggests that any mental health impacts were relatively minor. Medication was offered but declined by the Appellant.9 In addition, the notes state that the Appellant was suffering from XXXX XXXX since 2017, and although her mood was "worse since the death of her employer," the psychiatrist reports that her mental health was also negatively impacted by her "failed refugee hearing" as well as other problems such as losing her job, her inability to send money to her children and her husband's infidelity,10 indicating that any mental health condition was in existence well before the death of her employer, and may have worsened after her hearing. As noted in the letter, the consultation did not take place at the time when the Appellant was allegedly facing the impact of her employer's death, but rather over XXXX months later on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, which I find further limited the ability of the psychiatrist to assess the Appellant's mental state at the time of her RPD hearing.

[16] Based on these factors, I give the notes limited weight. Further, the report suggests that any mental health issues that the Appellant had pre-existed her employer's death, and were also impacted by events after her hearing, such as the outcome of her claim. I therefore find that the new evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that credibility issues arising from the Appellant's testimony can be explained by the impact of her employer's death on her mental health.

[17] The Appellant also submitted a letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 from XXXX XXXX,11 relief caregiver for the Appellant's client's family. The letter states that the Appellant had worked for this family for XXXX months and was close to the family. She opines that she "can imagine how emotionally impacted" the Appellant would have been by her client's death. While I consider this letter, I give it very limited weight regarding the Appellant's mental state, as Ms. XXXX had only briefly met the Appellant, and has no expertise regarding mental health and the Appellant's ability to provide testimony.

[18] For these reasons, I find that the Appellant has not established that the impact of her employer's recent death was responsible for her inability to provide consistent and credible evidence during her hearing. I also find that, based on my review, the panel was mindful of issues of trauma, noting that she would not be asking for details about the claimed sexual assault, and that the panel did check in and provide a break for the Appellant when needed.12 The Appellant does not specify what additional accommodations should have been provided or what else could have been done during her hearing. In addition, many of the RPD's credibility findings did not relate to the Appellant's testimony, memory or concentration, but rather also included other findings of a lack of expected corroboration and delay in claiming.
The RPD did not rush the Appellant's closing submissions or fail to pay adequate attention to her oral submissions

[19] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in rushing her legal representative in his closing submissions, and in failing to pay adequate attention to these submissions. She argues that
[t]he Member was pressed for time towards the end of the hearing's scheduled timeslot. When she asked Counsel to present his oral submissions, Counsel replied, "So I'm going to talk at length, but try and be as precise as I can, Madam Member." To which the Member replied, with a nervous laugh, "Not too much at length, it's a quarter to twelve. " The Member knew she would be reserving her decision, so it would have been prudent for her to instruct Counsel to not rush through oral submissions, and instead to send in written submissions following an agreed chronology. This would have allowed Counsel to thoughtfully review the testimony and other evidence given at the hearing and to deliver submissions that were properly linked to the evidence and relevant passages of case law. Instead of which, Counsel (who perhaps lacked the experience to ask the Member for the opportunity to make written submissions) rushed through his submissions at speed.13

[20] Based on my review of the record of the hearing, I disagree with this argument. First, the panel only made the comment, "not too much at length," in response to the legal representative's statement that he was "going to talk at length."14 I find that even if the panel cautioned the legal representative regarding the time, it does not appear that his oral submissions were cut short. I note that the Appellant's legal representative's oral closing submissions took approximately 25 minutes15 of the 2 hour and 46-minute-long hearing (or 7 pages of the 60-page transcript of the hearing16), which I find is in fact longer than the typical oral submissions at RPD hearings. The panel also granted the representative 10 minutes to gather his thoughts before he made his closing submissions, and a further opportunity at the end of the hearing on the request of the Appellant's legal representative to make a final point.17 Further, the closing submissions provided were extensive, and covered all of the issues in the appeal, including Convention grounds, the Appellant's cultural background and ear injury, caselaw on credibility, specific issues in the evidence regarding omissions and state protection, subjective fear and the Appellant's US refugee claim and delay in claiming, the alleged agents of persecution, objective country condition evidence and citations from the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Kenya, s.97 and generalized risk, state protection and IFA. Finally, the Appellant does not specify what issues were missed or what would have been presented had her representative not been rushed as alleged. I find that the RPD did not rush the Appellant's legal representative's closing submissions as argued by the Appellant.

[21] The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred in paying inadequate attention to the oral submissions made by her counsel, including Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) directives, Federal Court decisions and evidence of forward-looking risk from the NDP. I find, however, that she does not specify what has been ignored, and based on my review, I do not see that the RPD erred in this fashion as argued.
The RPD did not err in its credibility findings

[22] The RPD made a number of findings regarding the credibility of the Appellant's evidence, including that her testimony was vague and evolving; that there were significant inconsistencies and omissions in her evidence; and that she did not provide expected corroboration of her allegations; for example, of the claimed XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, such as media reports, police reports or a support letter from her husband or the mother who was the alleged victim of the crime, whom she claims she had been in touch with while in the US.

[23] With respect to her claim that she spoke out regarding women's health issues and the XXXX XXXX incident, the RPD found that the Appellant was evolving and unclear in her evidence about these allegations and inconsistent in the number of meetings that she spoke at. It found that she initially testified that she spoke only at a Chief's meeting in 2015, but then her evidence evolved to being a speaker six or seven times and then four times.

[24] The Appellant does not specifically challenge this finding, except regarding the issue of the impact of her mental health on her ability to testify, which I have addressed above. I agree with the RPD's inconsistency finding as outlined above, and that the Appellant's vague, evolving and inconsistent evidence regarding her role as a spokesperson on women's health issues, despite the efforts of the panel to prompt her and ask follow-up questions about this allegation, is damaging to the credibility of her allegations.

[25] Regarding her claims about the Chinkororo gang, the alleged agents of persecution, the RPD found that she omitted an allegation that members of the gang confronted her at the community meeting in 2015. It found that she was inconsistent regarding when the alleged threats began, testifying that they started before the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, at the local meeting where she spoke, but in her narrative stated that she came to their attention later after the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident. Further, it found that she did not provide corroborating evidence regarding the existence of the Chinkororo gang.

[26] The Appellant does not specifically challenge these findings except for her general argument that problems in her testimony were caused by her troubled state of mind because of the trauma of her employer's recent death, which I have found has not been established. Based on my review, I agree with the RPD's finding that her evidence about when the alleged threats began was inconsistent, and that there was a lack of corroboration about the Chinkororo gang, and that these factors reduce the credibility of her allegations.

[27] The RPD found that a hand-written letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2018 from an assistant chief's office about unknown people who allegedly attacked her home and "roughing up" her family to be unreliable, as she could not explain why her husband would report this alleged attack to the assistant chief instead of the police; her evidence was inconsistent, as she testified that the men just asked for her, but the letter states that the family was "roughed up;" and it was unclear who "the family" at the home was, as her adult children did not live there.

[28] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in this finding, as she claims that her sons were at the home following the funeral of her colleague, and because of cultural differences and beliefs about police corruption, it was reasonable to report the attack to the chief, who plays a role in maintaining order in the community. Even if this is the case, I agree with RPD's finding that her testimony was inconsistent with the description of the attack in the letter, as she testified that they were not assaulted as follows:
CLAIMANT: It's my husband who was harassed. For them they were asked, where is your mum.
MEMBER: How was your husband harassed? What do you mean by that?
CLAIMANT: How can I put it now? They told him --- they demanded to know where I am. They told him to open the house and then they entered and looked for me. When they didn't find me, they asked him, where is your wife who is the one we want. He told them ---
MEMBER: Did they touch him? Did they physically assault your husband?
CLAIMANT: They didn't assault him physical but they threw words to him.
MEMBER: Did they do anything to your children?
CLAIMANT: They didn't beat them.
MEMBER: Okay. So, it says, "unknown assailants attack his home, roughing up his family". What does that mean? That means that they roughed up your family.
CLAIMANT: They put them together and wanted to know where I am but they could have maybe also reacted. The way they were, they could beat them that night.
MEMBER: They beat them that night?
CLAIMANT: They could beat them.
MEMBER: They could beat them but they didn't. Did they beat them?
CLAIMANT: No.
MEMBER: It says they roughed your family so that's why I want to know what that means.
CLAIMANT: Can you explain to me that?
MEMBER: It says, well, don't look at your --- It says here, "unknown assailants attacked his home roughing up his family." Roughing up his family so I was asking you what they do to rough up your family which means physical attack.
CLAIMANT: Roughing up to them is that, how can I put this? It's just pushing you here and there. Asking you where is this? Where is that?18
I agree with the RPD and find that this significant inconsistency between the letter and the Appellant's testimony reduces the credibility of this letter.
Delay

[29] The RPD also found that the Appellant's abandonment of her asylum claim in the US after living there for one and a half years also diminished the credibility of her subjective fear. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in this finding, as she did not feel safe or feel she would receive fair treatment there, but I disagree with this argument, and agree with the RPD that the fact that she left the US in the middle of her asylum claim to diminish her credibility. As noted by the Appellant, she had a nursing job there and had a roof over her head, and I find that her claim was ongoing, and she had no immediate fear of deportation or loss of status.
Lack of corroboration

[30] The RPD found that other expected corroboration was lacking, and that other corroborating evidence was unreliable. It found that there was a lack of corroboration of the alleged XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, and that this diminished the credibility of this claim. The Appellant testified that the incident was reported in the media, but provided no corroboration of this incident, and only submitted an article about a similar incident in 2016. In response to this concern, the Appellant testified that she had lost her phone and was unable to contact anyone to obtain corroborating evidence about this incident. She had also testified that she had spoken with the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX while she was in the US in 2018, however, her contact with the mother and her update on the police investigation was omitted from her narrative. Further, although allegedly in contact with her, she did not obtain any corroboration such as a letter or affidavit from her, even though the mother allegedly informed her that the investigation was ongoing, and that one person had been arrested. The RPD did not accept her explanation that she did not know that she should do that because of what she was undergoing.19 I agree with the RPD that the Appellant was inconsistent in her explanation for her lack of corroboration, as she said she could not contact anyone because she had lost her phone, but this was inconsistent with her evidence that she had been in touch with the mother of the XXXX XXXX. I agree that she did not adequately explain why she did not request corroboration of the XXXX XXXX XXXX incident, which was central to her claim.

[31] The Appellant argues that the RPD was illogical in noting that the news article provided was "eerily similar" to her own allegations, but even if that was the case, it does not change the fact that she provided no corroboration of this incident, which I find would have been expected.

[32] The RPD made a negative inference from the fact that the Appellant did not provide corroboration from her husband, who was allegedly attacked by unknown people and tried to get corroborating evidence. I agree with this negative inference.

[33] In general, negative inferences cannot be drawn solely from the failure to produce corroborating evidence, but the failure to provide corroboration can be considered when there are valid reasons to doubt the claimant's credibility20, or where the explanation for failing to provide this evidence when it would reasonably be expected is not accepted.21 I find that this is such a case, as there were credibility issues arising from the Appellant's evidence, and there was no good explanation provided for the lack of corroboration. The lack of corroboration of the XXXX XXXX incident, either from the media or from the alleged victim of the crime, with whom the Appellant was in contact, or corroboration from the Appellant's own husband of other allegations, such as the attack on him and on her co-worker, further reduces the credibility of these allegations.

[34] The RPD found that other corroborating documentation was insufficient to overcome its other credibility findings. The Appellant provided a funeral programme as corroborating evidence about the death of a colleague. The RPD found that this did not establish any connection between his death and the XXXX traffickers. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that there was no corroboration of how the death of her colleague was connected to the child traffickers, as he was going to be a witness about the incident, so it was natural for her to fear that it was connected to the crime. Although it appears that she is arguing that her conclusion that the killing of her former co-worker was connected to the crime is logical, I find that this still does not address the issue of a lack of evidence that the two incidents were connected and find that the RPD did not err.
Summary of findings

[35] In summary, I find that the RPD did not err in its credibility findings, and I agree with its determination that the Appellant has not credibly established her allegations on a balance of probabilities because of inconsistencies and omissions in her evidence, the abandonment of her US asylum claim, as well as a lack of expected corroboration. I find that this is determinative of her claim both regarding whether or not she is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection. As a result, it is unnecessary for me to further address the RPD's other findings or the Appellant's arguments in relation to state protection and IFA.
CONCLUSION

[36] On the basis of the findings outlined above, I dismiss the appeal. I find that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
